case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a second-in-time habeas filing that seeks to add/raise a new claim while appellate review of the district court’s judgment on the prisoner’s first federal habeas petition is still pending is a “second or successive” application requiring authorization under 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b) (AEDPA’s bar on “second or successive” habeas applications and its gatekeeping/authorization requirement).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Rivers (supported by multiple amici) argues that a habeas filing made during the pendency of an appeal from the judgment on the initial habeas case should be treated procedurally as part of the still-ongoing first habeas proceeding (i.e., an amendment/supplement or continuation), not as a new “second or successive” petition under § 2244(b). Petitioner’s side emphasizes that treating such a filing as “second or successive” is conceptually mistaken because the first habeas case is not final while on appeal; it creates arbitrary, non-uniform jurisdictional outcomes across circuits; it forces prisoners into inefficient and duplicative protective filings; and it increases burdens on courts and litigants—contrary to sensible AEDPA administration. Amici (former judges, prosecutors, defenders, and scholars) also stress administrability: a clear rule that filings during the appeal are not “second or successive” reduces satellite litigation over jurisdiction and avoids needless gatekeeping motions in the courts of appeals.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Texas (Lumpkin) argues that once the district court has entered judgment on the initial habeas petition, any later filing raising new habeas claims is properly treated as a “second or successive” application under § 2244(b), even if the prisoner has appealed the initial judgment. Respondent’s position is that AEDPA’s gatekeeping regime would be undermined if petitioners could add new claims after an adverse district-court judgment without complying with § 2244(b)’s authorization requirements; that finality and orderly process support a bright-line rule keyed to the district court’s judgment; and that allowing post-judgment claim additions during appeal risks gamesmanship, delay, and piecemeal litigation (precisely what AEDPA sought to limit).

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas make the strongest textual point: § 2244(b) contains no express “pending appeal” carveout, and Gonzalez often treats post-judgment, claim-advancing filings as successive. But Gonzalez’s anti-circumvention rule is best read as keyed to the completion of a habeas proceeding in the ordinary sense; treating a still-on-appeal first petition as already a concluded “application” would turn a nonfinal posture into a jurisdiction-stripping trigger without clear statutory command and would predictably force the protective § 2244(b) filings Justice Alito flags as administratively perverse. Banister’s rule-bound focus on what remains within the ordinary course of a single proceeding supports a narrow term-of-art reading here: appellate review is still part of that course even if the vehicle is not Rule 59(e), and we can reserve whether later, post-mandate claim additions or reopening efforts are successive. Magwood’s judgment baseline remains intact—no new state-court judgment exists—but it does not answer when the first federal opportunity ends, and a modest appellate-pendency rule minimizes traps while keeping AEDPA’s gatekeeping for truly later attempts.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s appeal-finality/administrability argument would require us to treat § 2244(b)’s “second or successive application” as if it said “after appellate review is complete,” but Congress did not write that limitation. Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Banister is unpersuasive under a textualist reading because Banister is expressly confined to a timely Rule 59(e) motion—an established, rule-bound continuation of the same case—not a post-judgment filing introducing new grounds, which Gonzalez identifies as successive in substance. Magwood reinforces that the relevant “reset” is a new state-court judgment, not the pendency of a federal appeal; allowing free-form new claims during appeal invites the very piecemeal litigation AEDPA was designed to curb. Practical “trap” concerns can be addressed through existing procedural mechanisms, but we cannot create an atextual pending-appeal carveout that alters AEDPA’s gatekeeping scheme.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s administrability point—that “one full opportunity” should include appeal and that our rule will prompt protective § 2244(b) filings—is serious, but it asks us to add an appellate-finality condition that § 2244(b) simply does not contain. As Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas emphasize, Gonzalez’s functional approach is triggered by substance: after the district court has entered judgment, a filing that advances a new ground operates as a new habeas “application,” and Banister’s narrow Rule 59(e) carveout underscores that only rule-bound, judgment-focused reconsideration stays within the first proceeding. Magwood’s judgment-centered framework likewise points to an intervening new state-court judgment as the relevant reset, not the pendency of federal appellate review. The practical “trap” concerns can be mitigated through existing procedural tools, but they do not justify creating an atextual pending-appeal exception to AEDPA’s gatekeeping.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas make the strongest point that § 2244(b) contains no express “pending appeal” exception and that Gonzalez treats post-judgment, claim-advancing filings as successive, but that reads Gonzalez’s anti-circumvention rule beyond its premise of a concluded habeas proceeding. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, when the first habeas judgment is still on direct appellate review, the petitioner’s first federal opportunity has not ended in the ordinary sense, and converting that nonfinal posture into a jurisdiction-stripping successiveness trigger risks arbitrary forfeitures—especially for unrepresented prisoners—while incentivizing protective, premature § 2244(b) motions. Banister, though tied to Rule 59(e), reinforces the term-of-art inquiry into what remains within a single proceeding’s ordinary course of review; appeal is part of that course, and courts can police gamesmanship through ordinary procedural tools without expanding AEDPA’s gatekeeping to mid-appeal supplementation. Magwood’s judgment-based framework still fits because the attacked state-court judgment is the same; the question is when the first federal “application” is complete, and pegging that to the conclusion of appellate review is the more coherent and fair boundary.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas press the hardest textual point: § 2244(b) does not say “pending appeal,” and Gonzalez treats post-judgment, claim-advancing filings as new applications in substance. But Gonzalez’s anti-circumvention rule presupposes a habeas proceeding that has reached ordinary completion; as Chief Justice Roberts argues, keying “second or successive” to a district-court judgment still on direct appellate review would convert a nonfinal posture into a jurisdictional gate without a clear statutory signal and would predictably force protective § 2244(b) motions that undermine AEDPA’s administrability. Banister’s emphasis on what remains within the ordinary course of a single proceeding supports treating appellate review as part of that same “application,” while still allowing courts to deny amendment, consolidate, or sanction to deter gamesmanship. Magwood’s judgment baseline is not displaced: the state-court judgment remains the same, but the better reading of “second or successive” as a term of art is that the first federal application is not complete until direct appellate review is over.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas present the strongest objection: § 2244(b) contains no explicit “pending appeal” exception, and Gonzalez warns that post-judgment filings adding new grounds can function as successive applications. But Gonzalez’s functional test presupposes a completed habeas proceeding in the ordinary course and was aimed at end-runs around finality; it does not clearly answer whether an “application” is over for § 2244(b) purposes while direct appellate review of the first judgment remains pending, as the Chief Justice emphasizes. Banister, though tied to Rule 59(e), reinforces the term-of-art inquiry into what remains within the ordinary course of a single proceeding; reading § 2244(b) to attach jurisdiction-stripping consequences to a nonfinal, still-on-appeal posture lacks a clear textual command and risks the “protective authorization” dynamic Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan describe. Magwood’s judgment-centric framework addresses what counts as a new attack (a new intervening state judgment), not when the first federal opportunity has concluded, so I do not see it as compelling respondent’s district-court-judgment bright line here.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s “one full opportunity” approach has real practical appeal, and I understand Justice Kagan’s concern about protective § 2244(b) filings and traps for pro se litigants, but I do not see a sufficiently firm anchor for an appellate-finality carveout in the statutory text or our cases. Justice Barrett’s point about Banister is especially persuasive under my methodology: Banister preserves only a narrow, rule-bound lane (timely Rule 59(e)) within the same proceeding, and it does not license free-form addition of new habeas grounds after judgment simply because an appeal is pending. Gonzalez’s functional rule, as Justice Thomas and Justice Alito emphasize, treats post-judgment filings advancing new claims as new applications in substance, and Magwood’s judgment-centered frame reinforces that the relevant reset is an intervening new state-court judgment—not continued federal appellate review. The equities can be addressed through ordinary tools (timely amendment before judgment, Rule 59(e), stay-and-abeyance) without creating an atextual pending-appeal exception that would be hard to administer and would dilute AEDPA’s anti-piecemeal design.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability and “one full opportunity” framing is the strongest point on the other side, but it effectively adds an appellate-finality condition that § 2244(b) does not supply; the statute asks whether the later filing is a second or successive “application,” not whether the first has run its entire appellate course. Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan read Gonzalez as limited to truly completed proceedings, yet Gonzalez’s core functional rule turns on substance—post-judgment filings that advance new grounds operate as new habeas applications—while Banister’s Rule 59(e) carveout confirms that only tightly rule-bound, judgment-directed reconsideration remains within the same application. Magwood’s judgment-centered baseline likewise does not support a pending-appeal exception because the relevant reset is an intervening new state-court judgment, not the continued pendency of federal appellate review. The “trap” concern is real, but under a textualist approach it is better addressed through existing procedural mechanisms rather than by creating an atextual exception to AEDPA’s gatekeeping.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas make the strongest case that § 2244(b) contains no express pending-appeal exception and that Gonzalez treats post-judgment, claim-adding filings as successive in substance. But that reading extends Gonzalez beyond its anti-circumvention context—an attempt to reopen a concluded federal habeas judgment—whereas a first petition still on direct appellate review is not practically “finished,” and, as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, anchoring the jurisdictional trigger to a nonfinal district-court disposition creates arbitrary traps and incentivizes protective § 2244(b) filings that undermine AEDPA’s orderly administration. Banister’s focus on what remains within the ordinary course of a single proceeding supports treating appellate review as part of that same habeas opportunity, while still allowing courts to police gamesmanship through ordinary procedural tools rather than an automatic, harsh gatekeeping bar. Magwood’s judgment-centered rule answers what judgment is being attacked, not when the first federal review of that judgment is complete, so it does not compel respondent’s post-judgment bright line here.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 2244(b)’s “second or successive” bar is best read to attach only after the prisoner has had one full opportunity for federal habeas review, and that opportunity is not complete while appellate review of the first petition remains pending. Treating a mid-appeal filing as “second or successive” elevates a district court’s judgment over the completion of appellate review in a way that is in tension with ordinary finality principles and invites needless gatekeeping litigation, undermining administrability and institutional legitimacy without clear statutory command. This narrower approach preserves AEDPA’s anti-piecemeal aims because district courts retain control over post-judgment amendments through the Federal Rules (as incorporated by § 2242) and can police delay or gamesmanship case-by-case. Consistent with this understanding, courts have held that a later filing is not “second or successive” until the first habeas proceeding—including appellate review—has concluded.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b) imposes a gatekeeping requirement on a "second or successive" habeas "application," and nothing in the statute creates an exception for filings made after the district court has entered final judgment merely because an appeal is pending. Once judgment has issued, a later filing that advances a new ground for relief is not a continuation of the first adjudication but a new collateral "application" attacking the same state-court judgment, and AEDPA’s structure favors a bright-line rule that prevents piecemeal litigation and preserves finality. This Court’s distinction between true post-judgment motions that are part of the same case and filings that "advance" new habeas claims supports treating Rivers’ filing as successive. See Gonzalez v. Crosby, 545 U.S. 524 (2005) (post-judgment filings advancing new habeas claims are successive) and Banister v. Davis, 590 U.S. 504 (2020) (Rule 59(e) is part of the first proceeding, unlike new-claim filings).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 2244(b) bars a "second or successive" application challenging the same state-court judgment unless the court of appeals authorizes it, and Congress adopted that gatekeeping rule to prevent piecemeal, repetitive litigation and to promote finality. Once the district court has entered judgment disposing of the first federal habeas petition, a later filing that advances a new ground for relief functions as a new habeas application and falls within Gonzalez v. Crosby’s rule that post-judgment filings advancing habeas "claims" are successive. Banister v. Davis is consistent because it treats a timely Rule 59(e) motion as part of the first proceeding’s single judgment, but Rivers’ new-claim filing is not such a narrow, rule-bound reconsideration device and would undermine AEDPA’s practical operation by inviting strategic claim-splitting during appeal. Magwood v. Patterson confirms the relevant baseline: § 2244(b) applies when the later application again challenges the same underlying state-court judgment, which this second-in-time filing does.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 2244(b)’s “second or successive” bar is a term of art, not a purely chronological label, and this Court has repeatedly looked to procedural posture and practical function to determine whether a filing is truly a new habeas “application.” See Slack v. McDaniel, 529 U.S. 473, 486 (2000); Banister v. Davis, 590 U.S. 504, 511–12 (2020). When the first habeas case is still under appellate review, treating a second-in-time filing that adds a new claim as part of the ongoing first proceeding better fits AEDPA’s purposes—promoting efficient, consolidated adjudication without forcing duplicative gatekeeping motions—while avoiding arbitrary outcomes that fall hardest on unrepresented and vulnerable prisoners. A district-court judgment pending appeal is not the kind of finality that justifies the harsh jurisdictional consequences of § 2244(b), and courts retain tools to prevent delay or gamesmanship without foreclosing potentially meritorious claims on technical grounds.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2244(b) triggers only when a prisoner files a new application that is properly characterized as “second or successive,” and our cases treat that phrase functionally rather than purely temporally. Under Gonzalez v. Crosby, a post-judgment filing is successive when it advances new habeas “claims,” but Banister v. Davis underscores that filings that are part of the ordinary course of a still-unfolding first proceeding are not “second or successive”; while an appeal is pending, the initial habeas litigation has not reached final resolution. Magwood v. Patterson’s judgment-focused approach reinforces that AEDPA’s gatekeeping targets repeat challenges after completion of the first habeas review of the same state-court judgment, and pegging successiveness to the end of appellate review better fits statutory coherence and workability by avoiding arbitrary circuit-by-circuit procedural traps without materially undermining AEDPA’s anti-piecemeal aims.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 2244(b)’s gatekeeping applies only to a “second or successive” habeas “application,” a term of art that takes its content from historical habeas practice rather than mere chronology. See 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b); Banister v. Davis, 140 S. Ct. 1698, 1705 (2020); Magwood v. Patterson, 561 U.S. 320, 332 (2010). When appellate review of the district court’s judgment on the first petition remains pending, the initial federal habeas proceeding is not yet complete in the ordinary sense, and a filing seeking to add a claim is best understood as part of that still-ongoing case—not the commencement of a new “application” triggering § 2244(b). Reading “second or successive” to attach at district-court judgment would create atextual, judge-made finality rule and expand AEDPA’s jurisdictional gatekeeping beyond its historically grounded scope; to the extent uncertainty remains in a statute restricting access to the writ, the better course is the narrower construction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 2244(b) establishes a strict gatekeeping regime for any later-in-time filing that advances a new habeas claim after the district court has entered judgment on the initial petition, and this Court in Gonzalez v. Crosby held that post-judgment filings that add or advance habeas claims function as successive applications in substance. Magwood v. Patterson reinforces a judgment-based framework: where the later filing challenges the same state-court judgment as the first, § 2244(b) applies absent an intervening new judgment. Banister v. Davis confirms that certain tightly cabined, ordinary post-judgment motions (like Rule 59(e)) are part of the first proceeding, but it does not authorize a broad end-run around § 2244(b) by raising new claims after judgment while an appeal is pending. A bright-line keyed to the district court’s judgment is more workable and better serves AEDPA’s finality and anti-piecemeal purposes, while still leaving petitioners the § 2244(b) authorization pathway for genuinely new claims.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 2244(b) applies to a later-in-time filing that, in substance, advances a new "claim" for habeas relief from the same state-court judgment, and its text contains no exception for filings made while an appeal from the first petition’s denial is pending. Under Gonzalez v. Crosby, a post-judgment filing that seeks to "add a new ground for relief" is functionally a habeas application and must be treated accordingly; allowing new claims after the district court’s judgment would permit circumvention of AEDPA’s gatekeeping regime. Banister v. Davis confirms that only limited, judgment-focused motions (Rule 59(e)) are part of the first proceeding, whereas adding new claims after judgment is not. Whatever the administrability concerns, the statute’s finality-focused design and our functional approach to post-judgment filings support treating Rivers’ second-in-time claim-raising filing as "second or successive" absent § 2244(b) authorization.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 2244(b)’s “second or successive” bar is a term of art and does not mechanically apply to every later-in-time filing; the Court has distinguished filings that are properly viewed as part of resolving the first habeas proceeding from truly successive applications. See Banister v. Davis, 590 U.S. 504 (2020). When appellate review of the initial habeas judgment is still pending, the habeas case is not practically final, and treating a new-claim filing as automatically “second or successive” risks arbitrary, circuit-dependent procedural traps and inefficient protective litigation—outcomes in tension with AEDPA’s administrability and with procedural fairness. While Gonzalez v. Crosby, 545 U.S. 524 (2005), flags that post-judgment filings advancing new “claims” can be successive, its logic is best read to target end-runs around final judgments; here, the continuing appeal supports treating the filing as a request to supplement/amend in the same proceeding rather than a new § 2244(b) application.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a habeas filing that raises new claims while the appeal of the judgment on the prisoner’s first federal habeas petition is still pending should be treated as a “second or successive” petition requiring circuit-court authorization under AEDPA.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b) (AEDPA’s limits on “second or successive” habeas corpus applications).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Rivers argues that a second-in-time filing submitted during the pendency of an appeal from the denial (or other disposition) of his initial federal habeas petition should not be deemed “second or successive” under § 2244(b) because the first habeas proceeding is not yet окончательно concluded; instead, the later filing should be treated functionally as an amendment/supplement to the still-ongoing first habeas case (or otherwise handled through ordinary procedural tools such as remand or relation-back principles) rather than being subjected to AEDPA’s gatekeeping regime. Petitioner-friendly amici (former prosecutors, federal judges, defenders, and scholars) emphasize that a contrary rule creates arbitrary outcomes driven by timing, burdens courts with unnecessary jurisdictional gatekeeping, and can force prisoners to choose between forfeiting newly discovered claims and risking dismissal under § 2244(b). They argue the Court should adopt a clear, uniform rule that minimizes needless procedural complexity and preserves a meaningful opportunity to present meritorious claims that arise before the first federal habeas process is fully finished.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Texas argues that once the district court has entered judgment on the initial federal habeas petition, any later filing asserting new grounds for relief is a new “application” and therefore qualifies as “second or successive” under § 2244(b), even if the earlier case is on appeal. Under that view, the prisoner must first obtain authorization from the court of appeals before the district court may entertain the new claims. Respondent’s position favors a bright-line, judgment-based cutoff to protect AEDPA’s finality, comity, and anti-serial-litigation purposes, preventing iterative claim-presentation and conserving judicial resources by enforcing the statute’s gatekeeping mechanism rather than allowing post-judgment ‘amendments’ to bypass § 2244(b).

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that a habeas case on appeal is “unfinished,” and Banister’s language about appeals as “further iterations” seems to support treating mid-appeal additions as part of the first application. But under my minimal, administrable approach, AEDPA’s trigger is best keyed to the district court’s entry of judgment: once judgment has issued, a later filing that advances new substantive habeas claims fits Gonzalez’s functional definition of a new “application,” and Banister’s carve-out is confined to tightly bounded, judgment-integrated mechanisms like timely Rule 59(e), not a freestanding claim-adding petition during appeal. Panetti’s functional exception for unripe claims does not justify an atextual “pending appeal” exception when the claims could have been raised earlier, and Magwood’s judgment-focused framework reinforces that absent a new intervening judgment, a second-in-time attack on the same conviction is successive. The equitable concerns Jackson raises about timing traps can be addressed through § 2244(b)’s authorization process and existing procedural tools, but those tools cannot negate Congress’s gatekeeping requirement without rewriting the statute.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that a pending appeal means the first habeas proceeding is still “unfinished,” and Banister’s “further iterations” language could be read to keep everything within one continuing case. But Banister ties that principle to tightly circumscribed, judgment-integrated mechanisms (timely Rule 59(e)), and does not authorize a free-standing, post-judgment filing that advances new substantive habeas claims; under Gonzalez, that kind of filing is a new habeas “application” in substance, which triggers § 2244(b)’s gatekeeping. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Panetti likewise does not carry the day because Panetti rests on a historically recognized ripeness exception (a claim that could not have been raised earlier), not an atextual “pending-appeal” exception that would rewrite Congress’s judgment-centered finality rule. Chief Justice Roberts’s administrable judgment-based line best reflects the statutory text and AEDPA’s design, leaving any broader equitable accommodation to Congress.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s and Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that an appeal means the first habeas case is still “unfolding,” so a mid-appeal filing could be treated as part of that ongoing proceeding via limited remand or indicative-ruling tools. But those case-management devices cannot redefine § 2244(b)’s trigger: once the district court has entered judgment, a later filing that advances new substantive habeas grounds is a new “application” in substance under Gonzalez, and AEDPA’s gatekeeping applies absent a new intervening judgment as Magwood frames it. Banister’s “iterations” language, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, preserves only traditional, tightly bounded, judgment-integrated mechanisms (like timely Rule 59(e)), not an open-ended claim-adding window during appeal. Panetti’s functional exception for unripe claims does not justify a general pending-appeal carveout untethered to text and would undermine AEDPA finality by inviting serial, post-judgment additions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Gonzalez-based bright line is the most serious objection, but Gonzalez addressed a closed habeas case where a Rule 60(b) motion sought to add merits claims after finality in the district court; it did not confront the different posture Justice Jackson highlights—where the first habeas proceeding remains under active appellate review and can be re-integrated via limited remand/indicative-ruling tools without serial, duplicative litigation. Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kagan’s judgment-centered reliance on Magwood and Banister is weighty, yet Magwood’s “new judgment” principle does not resolve when the first federal habeas process is “finished” for § 2244(b) purposes, and Banister’s term-of-art approach counsels against reading “second or successive” as a rigid chronology rule that creates arbitrary forfeiture during an appeal. The administrability concern is real, but it can be addressed by requiring a prompt showing of diligence and by allowing appellate courts to deny remand where supplementation would be abusive—rather than forcing vulnerable prisoners into § 2244(b) gatekeeping for claims discovered before the first application’s appellate iteration has concluded. Under my pragmatic approach, the equities and systemic costs of a timing trap during a pending appeal outweigh the marginal finality gains of treating this as a brand-new ‘application’ in the Gonzalez sense.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s best point is that a pending appeal means the first habeas proceeding is still “unfinished,” and Banister’s “further iterations” language offers a plausible way to fold mid-appeal developments into the first application through limited remands or indicative rulings. But Gonzalez’s functional test still fits: a freestanding post-judgment filing that “advances” new substantive habeas claims is a new “application” in substance, and Banister’s carve-out is expressly tied to tightly bounded, judgment-integrated mechanisms (like timely Rule 59(e)), not an open-ended mid-appeal claim-adding opportunity. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s administrable judgment-based line—reinforced by Magwood’s judgment focus—best preserves statutory coherence with § 2244(b)’s gatekeeping; case-management tools cannot supply an exception the statute does not. Panetti, as Justice Thomas notes, is better understood as a ripeness-based term-of-art exception and does not justify a broad “appeal pending” rule untethered to that limitation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s best point is that a case is not “finished” while an appeal is pending and that limited-remand/indicative-ruling tools could fold newly discovered claims into the original proceeding, avoiding arbitrary timing traps. But § 2244(b) speaks in terms of a later “application,” and under Gonzalez v. Crosby a post-judgment filing that advances new habeas claims functions as a new application in substance; treating the appeal as suspending that judgment-based trigger would create an atextual “appeal-pending” exception. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Panetti and Banister does not move me because Panetti’s non-successive category is tied to ripeness (a historically narrow exception) and Banister’s “further iterations” language is cabined to judgment-integrated vehicles like timely Rule 59(e), not a freestanding claim-adding filing after judgment. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Magwood’s judgment focus supplies an administrable line, and whatever equitable safety valve is desirable is for Congress to supply, not for us to redefine “application” to dilute AEDPA’s gatekeeping.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s best point is that a pending appeal means the first habeas proceeding is still “unfinished” and could be managed via limited remand or indicative rulings, but that case-management flexibility cannot override AEDPA’s judgment-centered gatekeeping once the district court has entered final judgment. Gonzalez v. Crosby is still the controlling functional line: a post-judgment filing that advances new substantive habeas claims is a successive application in substance, and Banister’s description of appeals as “further iterations” is best read—as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize—as limited to tightly bounded, judgment-integrated mechanisms like timely Rule 59(e), not an open-ended mid-appeal amendment window. Panetti’s term-of-art caution does not carry the day here because it addressed an unripe claim and a historically narrow exception, not a general appeal-pendency carve-out untethered to text and administrability. On an institutionalist, precedent-focused approach, the bright-line judgment rule (Roberts/Barrett) better preserves predictability and Congress’s finality design, leaving equities to § 2244(b)’s authorization pathways rather than judicially created exceptions.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s reliance on Banister’s description of appeals as “further iterations” of the first application is the strongest counter, but Banister’s holding is expressly tethered to Rule 59(e)’s traditional, judgment-integrated role; it does not create a free-floating rule that any new, claim-adding filing during an appeal remains part of the first “application.” Justice Sotomayor’s functional fairness point, invoking Panetti, also does not carry the day under the text: Panetti’s exception turns on ripeness and the term-of-art history, whereas here the prisoner is advancing additional habeas “claims” after entry of judgment, which Gonzalez instructs we must treat as a successive application in substance. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, a judgment-based line keyed to the district court’s final judgment is administrable and aligns with AEDPA’s gatekeeping design; any equitable mitigation can operate through § 2244(b)’s authorization mechanism rather than an atextual “pending appeal” exception. Magwood’s judgment focus reinforces that, absent a new intervening judgment, a later filing again attacking the same state-court judgment falls within § 2244(b).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Gonzalez-based bright line is the most serious counterpoint, but Gonzalez addressed Rule 60(b) reopening after the federal habeas judgment was effectively closed; it does not control a scenario in which the first application remains under active appellate review and can be handled through ordinary appellate management without treating the filing as a new “application.” Justice Barrett’s judgment-focused reading of Magwood strengthens the case for administrability, yet Magwood’s “new judgment” rule answers a different question (what counts as a new baseline judgment), not when the first federal habeas proceeding is finished for § 2244(b) purposes, and Panetti cautions against turning timing into forfeiture where the process is still ongoing. Justice Kagan is right to worry about an “open-ended amendment period,” but that concern can be addressed by limiting the rule to genuinely newly discovered/previously unavailable claims and by using remand/indicative-ruling tools and abuse-of-the-writ principles, rather than a categorical successive-label that creates a procedural trap with little added finality benefit. Under a procedural-fairness, consequence-sensitive approach, I cannot read § 2244(b)’s term of art to compel the harsh cutoff the Respondent proposes while an appeal is pending.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 2244(b) limits a "second or successive" habeas "application," and after the district court has entered final judgment on the first petition, a later filing asserting new substantive grounds for relief is best treated as a new application requiring court-of-appeals authorization. Under Gonzalez v. Crosby, a post-judgment filing that advances new habeas claims functions as a successive petition rather than a permissible continuation of the first case, and Magwood v. Patterson confirms § 2244(b) attaches when a later application again challenges the same state-court judgment. Banister v. Davis, which exempts Rule 59(e) motions as part of the original proceeding, underscores that only narrow, traditional, judgment-integrated mechanisms avoid § 2244(b); Rivers’ new-claim filing during appeal is not such a mechanism. A bright-line, judgment-based rule promotes AEDPA’s finality and comity interests while avoiding ad hoc appellate-management exceptions not grounded in the statute.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b) applies to any later “application” that is “second or successive” to an earlier federal habeas application challenging the same state-court judgment, and a filing asserting new grounds after the district court has entered judgment on the first application fits that description. Under Gonzalez v. Crosby, a post-judgment filing that advances new habeas “claims” is properly treated as a successive application, rather than an amendment, even if styled otherwise. Banister v. Davis confirms only that narrow, rule-bound reconsideration motions (Rule 59(e)) remain part of the first proceeding; it does not authorize new substantive claims post-judgment without § 2244(b) gatekeeping. Consistent with Magwood v. Patterson, because Rivers’ new filing attacks the same judgment as his first petition, it is “second or successive” and requires circuit authorization before any district-court consideration.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 2244(b) is triggered by a later “application” that asserts new grounds for habeas relief after the district court has entered judgment on the first petition; once judgment issues, a new filing advancing new claims is not a mere continuation of the first case but a new application subject to AEDPA’s gatekeeping. Gonzalez v. Crosby holds that a post-judgment filing that “advances” habeas claims must be treated as a successive petition, and nothing in AEDPA suggests that a pending appeal suspends that judgment-based line. While Banister v. Davis treats a Rule 59(e) motion as part of the original proceeding, that narrow carve-out does not extend to a freestanding second-in-time habeas filing raising new claims. Magwood v. Patterson reinforces that the “second or successive” inquiry is keyed to whether the later application challenges the same state-court judgment, which it does here, and practical consequences favor a bright-line rule that protects finality and prevents serial, iterative litigation against the same conviction.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 2244(b)’s “second or successive” bar is a term of art that does not apply to every later-in-time filing, and this Court has instructed that it must be construed in light of historical habeas practice rather than rigid formalism. Panetti v. Quarterman emphasized a functional approach to “second or successive,” and a filing presenting newly arisen or newly discovered claims while the first habeas case remains in active appellate review is best treated as part of the still-unfinished first proceeding, not as a new “application” triggering AEDPA’s gatekeeping. A judgment-based cutoff would create arbitrary, timing-driven forfeitures and disproportionately burden prisoners—often the most vulnerable—who uncover meritorious constitutional claims during the appellate window, undermining fairness and access to justice without materially advancing finality. Consistent with Magwood v. Patterson’s recognition that “second or successive” is not purely chronological, I would hold that such a filing is not “second or successive” under § 2244(b) and can be managed through ordinary procedural tools (e.g., remand or amendment principles) within the first habeas action.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 2244(b) imposes gatekeeping for any later “application” that is “second or successive,” and this Court has treated post-judgment filings that advance new habeas claims as successive in substance even when styled as something else. Under Gonzalez v. Crosby, a post-judgment filing that adds new grounds for relief functions as a new habeas application, while Banister v. Davis distinguishes only those limited, immediate post-judgment motions (like Rule 59(e)) that remain part of the first proceeding’s judgment. And Magwood v. Patterson ties the successive-inquiry to whether the filing challenges the same state-court judgment; here it does, so requiring circuit-court authorization is the most coherent and administrable reading that preserves AEDPA’s finality framework without turning appeals into open-ended amendment periods.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 2244(b) imposes gatekeeping on any later "application" that is "second or successive," and once the district court has entered judgment on the first habeas case, a new filing advancing new grounds for relief is best understood as a new application rather than an amendment. Gonzalez v. Crosby instructs that post-judgment filings that "advance" habeas claims function as successive applications, and Banister v. Davis confirms the limited set of true, judgment-integrated post-judgment motions (e.g., Rule 59(e)) that remain part of the first proceeding. Magwood v. Patterson further anchors the inquiry to whether the later application challenges the same state-court judgment; here it does, so § 2244(b)’s authorization requirement applies notwithstanding a pending appeal. Whatever equitable appeal petitioner offers, the statute’s text and the separation-of-powers limits on judicially crafted exceptions counsel enforcing Congress’s chosen bright-line gatekeeping rule.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 2244(b) bars a “second or successive” habeas “application” absent circuit authorization, and once the district court has entered judgment on the first petition, a later filing asserting new grounds for relief is best treated as a new application rather than a continuation of the first case. Gonzalez v. Crosby instructs that post-judgment filings that advance new habeas claims function as successive applications, and Banister v. Davis limits the non-successive category to narrow, judgment-integrated vehicles (like a timely Rule 59(e) motion) that are “part and parcel of the first habeas proceeding.” Magwood v. Patterson reinforces that the successive-petition inquiry is keyed to repeated challenges to the same state-court judgment, which is what Rivers is doing here. A bright-line, judgment-based rule is more workable and consistent with AEDPA’s finality and anti-serial-litigation purposes, leaving prisoners to seek authorization under § 2244(b) and courts to avoid end-runs around the gatekeeping regime.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 2244(b) applies to a “second or successive” habeas “application,” and our cases treat that phrase as a term of art that generally turns on whether the prisoner is again seeking federal habeas relief from the same state-court judgment. Magwood v. Patterson held that § 2244(b) is judgment-focused—i.e., it governs a later application “challenging the same state-court judgment”—and here the new filing raises new grounds for relief after the district court has entered judgment on the first petition, even if an appeal is pending. Under Gonzalez v. Crosby, a post-judgment filing that advances new habeas claims is functionally a successive application rather than a mere continuation of the first proceeding, and nothing in Banister v. Davis (limited to Rule 59(e) as part of the original judgment) extends that carveout to a second-in-time, claim-adding petition filed after judgment. A bright-line judgment-based rule best accords with AEDPA’s text and structure, requiring circuit authorization before a district court may entertain new claims in a second-in-time application challenging the same conviction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 2244(b)’s gatekeeping applies to truly new habeas “applications,” but a filing made while appellate review of the first habeas judgment is ongoing is best understood as part of the still-unfinished first application, not a separate, serial attack. In Banister v. Davis, the Court explained that “appeals from the habeas court’s judgment … are not second or successive; rather, they are further iterations of the first habeas application,” which supports treating mid-appeal efforts to add claims as an offshoot of that same proceeding rather than a new § 2244(b) petition. A judgment-based cutoff would create arbitrary timing traps and incentivize forfeiture of newly discovered, potentially meritorious claims, undermining procedural fairness without materially advancing AEDPA’s finality interests when ordinary tools (e.g., indicative-ruling/limited-remand procedures under Fed. R. Civ. P. 62.1 and Fed. R. App. P. 12.1) can manage supplementation efficiently. Construing “second or successive” to exclude these mid-appeal filings better harmonizes AEDPA with fair process and practical consequences in the criminal justice system.
